cues.text: Let us turn now to data categories and collection mechanisms.
Before we can talk about protecting personal data, we need to understand what kinds of data organisations hold, and how they come to hold it.
Each category carries its own risks.
The source organises this in a table with three columns: Data category, Example, and Risks.
Please look at the accompanying table as I walk through it row by row.
Row one.
The category is provided data, also called active data.
This is information that people knowingly give.
The examples are a profile, uploads, messages, and likes.
The risks are disclosure, harassment, and secondary use.
Secondary use means the data being used for a purpose other than the one for which the person gave it.
Row two.
The category is observed data, also called passive data.
This is data captured as people use a service, without them actively typing it in.
The examples are clicks, dwell time, IP address, and device events.
Dwell time is how long a person lingers on a page or item.
The risk listed is invisible monitoring, because the person often has no idea it is happening.
Row three.
The category is derived data, also called inferred data.
This is data that is worked out from other data.
The examples are interests, predicted income, and political leaning.
The risks are incorrect or sensitive profiling.
Notice the two dangers here: the inference may simply be wrong, or it may touch on sensitive matters the person never disclosed.
Row four.
The category is metadata.
The examples are time, location, sender and recipient, and device.
The risk is that metadata reveals patterns and relationships even without message content.
So you do not need to read someone's messages to learn a great deal about them.
Row five.
The category is third-party data.
The examples are contact uploads, partner SDK data, and broker data.
SDK stands for software development kit, a bundle of code that an app developer includes from another provider.
The risks are collection of nonusers and cross-context use.
Think about it: when someone uploads their phone contacts, the people in that list never agreed to anything, and they may not even use the service.
Cross-context use means data collected in one setting being used in a different one.
Now let us look closely at metadata.
The source defines metadata simply as data about data.
A timestamp and a location can reveal habits or visits.
Communication metadata can reveal associations, meaning who talks to whom.
The source then makes an important point about encryption.
End-to-end encryption protects message content between endpoints, under its design.
But it does not necessarily conceal metadata, device compromise, backups, or recipient actions.
So if a message is end-to-end encrypted, the content may be protected in transit, yet the fact that a message was sent, when, and between whom may still be visible.
A compromised device, a backup, or the recipient sharing the message are separate weaknesses that encryption between endpoints does not necessarily address.
Next, the mechanisms of collection, beginning with cookies and related tools.
Cookies store or reference browser state.
First-party cookies may support sessions, for example keeping you logged in.
Third-party cookies and other identifiers can enable cross-site tracking, which means following a person across different websites.
Tracking pixels generate requests when content is loaded, so simply opening a page or email can signal back to a server.
Mobile SDKs can collect app events.
Device permissions can expose contacts, location, and the microphone, where those permissions are granted or abused.
Then there is browser fingerprinting.
This combines browser and device attributes into a probabilistic or persistent identifier, and it can sometimes survive ordinary cookie deletion.
This leads to a misconception the source warns us to avoid: that clearing cookies removes all tracking.
It does not.
Server-side tracking and account identifiers also complicate user control.
If you are logged into an account, or if tracking happens on the organisation's servers rather than in your browser, deleting cookies does little.
Finally, application programming interfaces, or APIs.
APIs enable authorised data exchange between services.
The risks arise from excessive scopes, permissive defaults, inadequate review, or onward transfers, which means passing data on to further parties.
The source gives the controls: enforce minimal scopes, use revocable tokens, make access purpose-bound, carry out audits, and apply vendor controls.
In plain terms, give each integration only the access it needs, make that access withdrawable, tie it to a stated purpose, check it regularly, and hold vendors to account.
The last point concerns scraping.
Scraping public content can create new privacy risks through aggregation, face recognition, and cross-context use.
Collecting scattered public items into one profile creates something new and potentially harmful.
And the source closes with a key principle: public access does not equal unrestricted lawful processing.
That something is visible to anyone does not mean anyone may collect and use it however they wish.
